Courses/Docker from the kernel up

Puzzle 1 · 2 of 8

One kernel, or many?

Puzzle 0's container is a process on the host's kernel. So which kernel does it really use, the host's or one that came with its image? And how is that different from a virtual computer?

  • Puzzle 0: A container is a process

    A container is an ordinary process, started from an image's files, that the kernel runs like any other one; the host's ps lists it with its own PID. What makes it a container is a fence the kernel puts around it, limiting what it can see and how much it can use.

The problem

Puzzle 0 found the container's sleep in the host's process list, standing on the host's kernel. But the image was Alpine, a different Linux from the host's Ubuntu. Did Alpine bring its own kernel along? If you have used an Android emulator, you've run a whole second phone on your laptop, with its own operating system. Is a container like that?

It matters the day something depends on the kernel: a feature your program needs, a bug report that names a kernel version, or a container that works on a Linux server but behaves differently on your Mac.

See it

The building block

A process can compute on its own memory, but nothing more. To open a file, send a packet, or start another program, it must ask the kernel. That request is a system call: the program stops, the kernel does the work (or refuses), and the program carries on with the answer. Every process on a Linux machine, container or not, talks to the kernel only this way.

So the question "which kernel does a container use?" becomes "who answers its system calls?". uname -r answers it: it asks the kernel for its version with one system call and prints the answer. Next to it, read /etc/os-release, a file that names the Linux distribution whose files you're looking at. On the run behind this page:

Where it ranuname -r printed/etc/os-release said
On the host6.18.44-fc-v726Ubuntu 24.04.5
Inside the Alpine container6.18.44-fc-v726Alpine Linux v3.20

The files differ: each side reads its own copy of /etc/os-release (puzzle 3 shows how). The kernel doesn't: there is only one. An image holds the files of a Linux distribution, its programs and libraries, but no kernel to run. This has consequences you will meet:

  • Every container on a machine shares that machine's kernel, its version, its features and its bugs. A program that needs a newer kernel feature fails in a container on an older host, whatever image it came from.
  • There's nothing to boot. Starting a container is starting a process, which is why it takes about a second.
  • Linux containers need a Linux kernel to share. macOS and Windows don't have one.

A virtual machine (VM) is the other way to isolate a program: a whole pretend computer that boots its own operating system, kernel included. Its programs' system calls go to its own kernel. Under the VMs runs a hypervisor, the program that runs them and gives each its own pretend hardware: processors, memory, disks. The Android emulator runs as one: Android's documentation says a hypervisor manages it.

The two isolate at different places. Docker's documentation puts the trade-off plainly: a VM's isolation is stronger, because containers sharing a kernel are separated only by that kernel, while VMs are separated by the hardware boundary the hypervisor creates. The puzzles after this one show how that kernel draws its fences.

That's also what happens on your laptop. On a Mac or Windows machine, Docker Desktop starts a small Linux VM and runs your containers inside it, on its Linux kernel. So the Mac's own ps never lists your container's process: it's a process inside the VM. And uname -r in a container there prints the VM's kernel version, not anything about macOS.

The analogy

Puzzle 0's apartment block has one caretaker for every flat: whatever a household needs, it rings the same caretaker, and a household that moved in with its own furniture (Alpine's files) still rings him. A VM is a separate house on the same street, with its own caretaker. Docker Desktop on a Mac builds one small house with a Linux caretaker, and puts all your flats inside it.

Run it yourself

Before running, predict whether the two uname -r lines will match, and whether the two /etc/os-release lines will.

uname -r
docker run --rm alpine:3.20 uname -r
grep PRETTY /etc/os-release
docker run --rm alpine:3.20 grep PRETTY /etc/os-release

--rm removes the container when its program exits. Output from the run behind this page, on a Linux host:

6.18.44-fc-v726
6.18.44-fc-v726
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS"
PRETTY_NAME="Alpine Linux v3.20"

On a Mac, the first command reports the Mac's own kernel and the second reports the Linux kernel of Docker Desktop's VM, so they won't match. Try both, and you've seen the VM.

Check yourself

An image made from an older Linux distribution runs on a host whose kernel is 6.18.44. What does uname -r print inside the container?

Not quite. The image brought that distribution's files, not its kernel; the host's kernel answers.

Right. One kernel answers every container's system calls.

Not quite. uname -r makes a system call, and the shared kernel answers it.

Why does a container start in about a second, while a VM takes much longer?

Not quite. A container has no kernel of its own to boot at all.

Not quite. Starting a container starts a process; nothing ran before it. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Starting a container is starting a process.

On your Mac, Docker Desktop runs a container with sleep 1000. Does the Mac's own ps list sleep?

Not quite. The Mac's ps lists only macOS processes; sleep runs inside the VM.

Not quite. On a Mac the containers' host is the Linux VM, not macOS.

Right. On a Mac, the containers live in Docker Desktop's VM.

Sources
  • Docker docs: What is a container? ("Every VM boots its own complete operating system, including its own kernel, the core of the operating system that talks to the hardware."; "It’s still a process, so every container on a machine shares that machine’s kernel. There is no operating system to boot, which is why a container starts in about a second"; "The trade-off is that a VM’s isolation is stronger: containers that share a kernel are separated by that kernel, while VMs are separated by the hardware boundary the hypervisor creates."; "on macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs your Linux containers inside a small Linux VM that it manages for you, because Linux containers need a Linux kernel to share.")
  • Android Developers: Configure hardware acceleration for the Android Emulator ("VM acceleration uses your computer's processor to significantly improve the execution speed of the emulator. A tool called a hypervisor manages this interaction")
  • Linux manual: syscalls(2) ("The system call is the fundamental interface between an application and the Linux kernel.")
  • Linux manual: uname(2) ("uname() returns system information"; the field release is the "Operating system release")
  • The table and the output under Run it yourself were produced in this session with Docker Engine 29.9.2 on Linux 6.18.44 (Ubuntu 24.04 host), image alpine:3.20. The Mac behaviour in the last paragraph was not run here; it follows from Docker's statement above.

What you now know

A container brings files, not a kernel: every system call its process makes goes to the host's one kernel, so uname -r prints the host's version. A virtual machine boots its own kernel on a hypervisor. On a Mac or Windows laptop, Docker Desktop runs a Linux VM and your containers live inside it.
